title: Pawtograder · Realtime Fanout

panels.title: Connection cap utilisation
panels.description: Cluster connections as a fraction of the tenant's max_concurrent_users. This is the number that took production down on 2026-09-22: it sat at 1.00 for 47 minutes while every new websocket was refused with ConnectionRateLimitReached, and nothing on this dashboard showed it. Numerator uses max(), not sum(): realtime_connections_connected_cluster is a cluster-wide total that EVERY replica reports identically, so sum() would multiply it by the replica count.

panels.title: Connections (cluster)
panels.description: Live cluster-wide websocket count for the tenant. max() across replicas — each replica reports the same cluster total.

panels.title: Connection cap
panels.description: max_concurrent_users from realtime.tenants, exported by postgres_exporter. Read from the DATABASE rather than a chart value on purpose: the row is seeded once by SEED_SELF_HOST and drifts, and a hardcoded denominator would have shown false headroom throughout the 2026-09-22 outage.

panels.title: Tenant DB pool in use
panels.description: realtime_connect backends open against the configured db_pool. One node owns this pool for the WHOLE deployment; every private-channel authorization transaction and every realtime.messages read/write serialises through it. Saturation here precedes a tenant-connection kill.

panels.title: Connections vs cap (cluster)
panels.description: Connected clients against the tenant ceiling. When these two lines touch, new connections are being refused — not queued. Watch the gap, not the absolute value.

panels.title: Channel joins/s vs cap
panels.description: Cluster join rate against max_joins_per_second. sum(rate(...)) here — unlike the connection gauge, joins are a per-replica counter. A reconnect storm after a pod restart spikes this, which is why the join cap must be raised whenever the connection cap is.

panels.title: Broadcast throughput vs cap
panels.description: Socket bytes/s against max_bytes_per_second. Input and output are shown separately; the cap line is for reference against outbound fanout.

panels.title: realtime_connect pool: in use vs size
panels.description: The single tenant pool. Upstream defaults this to 1 connection, which is what let a burst queue past DBConnection's 5s queue_target on 2026-09-22 — Realtime counts those as database timeouts and answers by killing the tenant connection, tearing down Broadcast Changes replication for every user on every pod.

panels.title: Slow read-authorization checks
panels.description: Fraction of read-authorization checks falling outside the 250 bucket. Deliberately expressed as a bucket ratio rather than a quantile: the upstream histogram has only three boundaries (10 / 250 / 5000) and does not document its unit, so a histogram_quantile() here would be false precision. This is the leading indicator for pool saturation — auth checks queue behind realtime_connect before anything else breaks.

panels.title: Tenant connection owner
panels.description: Which replica currently holds the tenant's database connections (realtime_connect, the RLS checker, and the Broadcast Changes replication stream). Exactly one should be 1. Flapping means the tenant connection is being killed and re-initialised — the shape of the IncreaseConnectionPool incident. A graceful recycle happens roughly every 4h and is normal.

panels.title: Phoenix connections
panels.description: Aggregate Phoenix connection count across all realtime replicas. Tracks active WebSocket + HTTP keepalive sessions.

panels.title: Tenants connected
panels.description: Distinct Supabase realtime tenants with at least one active client. Self-hosted pawtograder has one tenant per deploy.

panels.title: Erlang reductions / s
panels.description: Reduction-count delta across all realtime replicas — a coarse proxy for VM workload (every function call increments reductions).

panels.title: Realtime memory by kind
panels.description: beam_memory_*_total_bytes — processes is the dominant share under load; binary signals large message buffers; ets is the in-memory state.

panels.title: Erlang VM activity
panels.description: Process and port counts indicate concurrency level. Run-queue depth > 0 sustained means a scheduler is backlogged.

panels.title: Realtime pod CPU (host view)
panels.description: osmon reads /proc; osmon_cpu_util is the per-replica utilization fraction. RAM lives on the Stack Overview dashboard (different unit / scale, doesn't compose with percentunit on the same axis).

panels.title: GC reclaimed bytes / s
panels.description: Rate of bytes reclaimed by the BEAM garbage collector — proxy for GC pressure.

description: Tenant quota + capacity panels (ids 100-141) added 2026-09-22 after two incidents this dashboard could not have shown: a 47-minute outage at max_concurrent_users=200 (ConnectionRateLimitReached), and a tenant-connection kill caused by a realtime_connect pool of 1 (IncreaseConnectionPool). The ceilings come from postgres_exporter's pawtograder_realtime_tenant collector reading realtime.tenants directly, NOT from chart values — a hardcoded denominator would have drawn reassuring headroom through both. PRIOR NOTE: DELETED 2026-09-04 (WS-APP): the two web_realtime_broadcast_total panels ("Server broadcasts / s" and "Server-initiated broadcasts by channel class") are gone rather than retargeted at a postgres_exporter query. Three reasons, in order. (1) The only trigger-side row a broadcast produces is an insert into realtime.messages, which is DAILY-PARTITIONED with short retention — a COUNT over it falls every time a partition is dropped, and Prometheus reads a falling counter as a reset, so it cannot back a rate() panel at all. (2) The windowed-gauge alternative means scanning the highest-write table in the database on every scrape, which is precisely the database_ram_metrics() pathology that cost 77.7% of production DB execution time (see the SCOPE block in supabase/functions/metrics/index.ts). (3) channel_class would have to be reconstructed by parsing realtime.messages.topic, which embeds class and resource ids, so the label would be loosely bounded by user-controlled data. Everything else on this dashboard comes from the realtime container's own /metrics endpoint (job="pawtograder-realtime"); if broadcast counts are wanted back, that is where they belong, not in a database scan.
